summary: Defines a NETCONF data model, in YANG, that monitors the NETCONF protocol itself, including datastores, sessions, locks, and statistics. It also defines ways for clients to discover which data models a server supports.

eli5.summary: This lets a network management tool ask a device about its own management connection: who is connected, what is locked, and what it understands.

questions: how to discover netconf supported schemas
what is the netconf monitoring yang module
what does get-schema do in netconf
how do netconf clients discover supported schemas
subtitle: A YANG data model that lets a NETCONF client inspect the server's sessions, locks, counters and supported schemas.

tldr.problem: A NETCONF client needs a standard way to see the state of the NETCONF server itself and to find and fetch the data models the server supports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a read-only YANG module with a netconf-state tree covering capabilities, datastores, schemas, sessions and statistics, plus a new get-schema operation to retrieve a schema.
tldr.outcome: Clients can list active sessions, see who holds locks, read counters and download supported schemas over NETCONF. The data is read-only and some of it is sensitive.

today: RFC 6022 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Monitoring Model
sections.content:
RFC 6022 defines a YANG (RFC 6020) model for monitoring the NETCONF protocol (RFC 4741). It gives information about NETCONF sessions and supported schemas.

Different schema formats, optional features and access controls can all change how much a server tells a client during session setup. The methods here give clients further ways to query schema and state information. They complement the existing base capabilities and operations and, in the RFC's words, in no way affect existing behaviour. A new <get-schema> operation lets a client retrieve schemas over NETCONF.

A server that implements the model, identified by the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-netconf-monitoring, MUST advertise that capability URI.
sections.eli5: It is like a dashboard on a machine that shows who is using it and what it can do, so you do not have to guess.

sections.title: The netconf-state Tree
sections.content:
The netconf-state container is the root of the monitoring data model. It has five subtrees: capabilities, datastores, schemas, sessions and statistics. Everything in the module is read-only.

The capabilities list MUST include all capabilities exchanged during session setup that still apply. The datastores list names the supported datastores (candidate, running, startup) and shows their lock state, for both global locks and partial locks (RFC 5717). For a partial lock it gives the locked nodes and the select expressions originally used. A lock held by a session not managed by the NETCONF server, such as a CLI session, is reported with session id 0.
sections.eli5: The device keeps one folder with five labeled pockets: what it can do, where its settings live, which rulebooks it knows, who is connected, and some tallies.

sections.title: Schemas, Sessions and Statistics
sections.content:
Each entry in schemas is keyed by identifier, version and format. For YANG, the identifier is the module or submodule name and the version is the most recent revision statement, or an empty string if there is none. Multiple versions MAY be supported at once and each MUST be listed individually. The model defines the formats xsd, yang, yin, rng and rnc. A location gives one or more places to fetch the schema, and the list SHOULD hold at least one entry.

The sessions list MUST include all active sessions. Each has a session-id, transport, username, source-host, login-time and counters in-rpcs, in-bad-rpcs, out-rpc-errors and out-notifications. The transport identities are netconf-ssh, netconf-soap-over-beep, netconf-soap-over-https, netconf-beep and netconf-tls.

The statistics subtree has server-wide counters: netconf-start-time, in-bad-hellos (sessions silently dropped because of an invalid hello), in-sessions, dropped-sessions (abnormally terminated, for example by idle timeout or transport close), plus the same four RPC counters as a session.
sections.eli5: Each rulebook is listed by name, edition and language. Each visitor gets a card with their name, when they arrived and how many requests they made.

sections.title: The get-schema Operation
sections.content:
The new <get-schema> operation retrieves a schema from the server. It takes a mandatory identifier, an optional version and an optional format that defaults to yang. The positive response is the requested schema.

If the schema does not exist, the error-tag is invalid-value. If more than one schema matches, the error-tag is operation-failed and the error-app-tag is data-not-unique.

A client normally first reads /netconf-state/schemas with <get>. That reply lists identifier, version, format and location but not the schema content. A location can be a URI for another protocol such as ftp or http(s), or the special value NETCONF, meaning the schema can be fetched with <get-schema>.
sections.eli5: First you ask for the catalog of rulebooks. Then you ask for one rulebook by name, and the device hands it over.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's examples show a <get> with a subtree filter on netconf-state and schemas. The reply lists schemas foo versions 1.0 and 1.1 in xsd format and bar and bar-types version 2008-06-01 in yang format, each with locations including NETCONF.

The examples then fetch foo 1.0 in xsd, bar by identifier and version, and bar-types by identifier alone, which returns the latest revision in the default YANG format.
sections.eli5: The examples show asking for the list, then picking one item from it by name and edition.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH (RFC 4742). Some readable nodes may be sensitive in some networks, so read access (via get, get-config or notification) should be controlled.

The one node the RFC singles out is /netconf-state/sessions/session/username. It holds identity information that could be used in an attempt to authenticate. It is meant for monitoring and SHOULD NOT be used for other purposes such as access control; two servers might report the same username for different people.

IANA registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-netconf-monitoring in the IETF XML Registry and the module ietf-netconf-monitoring with prefix ncm in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.eli5: The list of who is connected is private, so only trusted people should read it.
